analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover colorectal cancer screening for people over 50 and those at high risk.
analysis.headline: Backed by 25 senators from both parties and approved by the Senate Health Committee in 2002, the bill was placed on the Senate calendar but never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the nation's health insurance laws to require group health plans, employer plans, and individual health insurance to cover colorectal cancer screening at regular intervals for anyone 50 or older and for younger people at high risk, following the same screening methods and frequencies that Medicare covers. Colon cancer was the second-leading cause of cancer deaths in the U.S., and screening can catch it early enough to save lives, but too few people got screened because tests like colonoscopies are expensive. The bill also required the Labor and Health and Human Services departments to write and enforce the rules together.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured Americans age 50 and over and younger people at high risk for colorectal cancer, who would no longer face out-of-pocket barriers to colonoscopies and other screening tests that can catch cancer early.

how_it_helps.text: Requires group health plans, group insurance, and individual-market insurance to cover colorectal cancer screening at regular intervals for everyone 50 or older and for anyone under 50 at high risk.
Requires plans to cover the screening methods and frequency that Medicare covers, as determined appropriate by the patient's physician in consultation with the patient.

The bill's findings state that colorectal cancer was expected to kill about 56,600 Americans in 2002, that appropriate screenings can save large numbers of lives through earlier identification, and that too few Americans are screened according to widely accepted guidelines.
Does not override state laws that give patients stronger screening-coverage protections than the federal standard.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers that sponsor group health plans bear the added cost of covering screening tests, which flows into premiums and benefit costs.

drawbacks.text: Mandating coverage adds to insurers' and employers' benefit costs, which are generally passed along to consumers and workers through higher premiums.

The committee-amended version narrowed eligibility: the introduced bill covered younger people who had symptoms or circumstances indicating a need for screening, while the reported bill covered only those defined as high risk.

The committee version caps screening frequency at no more than Medicare's schedule unless the Health Secretary finds a different frequency would not reduce effectiveness, which could limit some physician-recommended tests.
Adding benefits to individual-market insurance can raise those premiums, which may lead some healthy people to drop coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is strong: screening for the nation's second-leading cancer killer saves lives, and the bill tied coverage to Medicare's established methods and frequency limits to guard against overuse. The cost is real but modest and spread across premiums. The main design tradeoff is the committee amendment, which narrowed coverage for symptomatic younger patients and set the requirements to start in 2003. On balance a fairly measured mandate whose biggest flaw was that it never became law.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Health Committee approved it in the summer of 2002 and it was placed on the Senate's calendar of pending business, but the chamber never brought it up for a vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003, so it died with the session.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on April 5, 2001, with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors that included Republicans Jesse Helms, Thad Cochran, Sam Brownback, Pat Roberts, and Olympia Snowe, along with Majority Leader Tom Daschle.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat for more than a year before a markup session in June 2002.

On July 10, 2002, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and it was formally reported on August 28, 2002, with a written report (No. 107-245); minority views were filed by committee members of the other party.
Twenty-five senators cosponsored the bill: 9 of the 49 Senate Republicans, 15 of the 49 Senate Democrats, and 1 of the 2 Independents.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 555) on August 28, 2002, but the Senate never took it up, and the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 without a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers were spared a new coverage mandate, while the roughly 56,000 Americans expected to die of colorectal cancer each year, and the many more who would have had it caught early, got nothing; patients kept bearing the cost of screening out of pocket.

industries.note: The bill would force insurers in both the group and individual markets to pay for colorectal cancer screening on Medicare-like terms, adding benefit costs they would pass into premiums. Their interest in avoiding the mandate ran against the screening coverage patients wanted.

ERISA group health plans would have to add screening coverage beginning with plan years starting in 2003, raising benefit costs for employers and unions. Grandfathering delayed the cost for plans under existing collective bargaining agreements.

industries.industry: Screening providers (gastroenterologists, endoscopy centers, and medical labs)
industries.note: Universal coverage for colonoscopies and other screening tests would send more patients to screening providers, and the same tests that generate their revenue are the ones that catch cancer early.
